clinicalPearls: Mansonelliasis is a filarial infection caused by Mansonella species (M. perstans, M. ozzardi, M. streptocerca) transmitted by biting midges and blackflies
It is endemic across parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and the Caribbean and Latin America, often coexisting with other filariases
Most infections are asymptomatic or cause mild, non-specific complaints, so the parasite is frequently an incidental finding
When symptomatic, features may include itching, transient swellings, arthralgia, serous-cavity involvement and, with M. streptocerca, skin changes
Peripheral eosinophilia is common and may be the clue that prompts investigation
Diagnosis rests on detecting microfilariae in blood or skin, depending on species; M. perstans and M. ozzardi produce blood microfilariae while M. streptocerca is found in skin
Treatment differs by species and often involves agents such as diethylcarbamazine or ivermectin, with doxycycline used against Wolbachia-harbouring species
reference.pathophysiology: Mansonella infection begins when infective larvae are inoculated by biting midges (Culicoides) or blackflies during a blood meal. The larvae mature into adult worms that reside in serous cavities, mesentery or subcutaneous tissue depending on the species, and release microfilariae into the blood or skin. Many species harbour Wolbachia endosymbiotic bacteria that contribute to inflammatory responses. Because the parasite provokes relatively little tissue reaction in most hosts, infection is often clinically silent; symptomatic disease reflects localised inflammatory and hypersensitivity responses to the worms and microfilariae, frequently accompanied by eosinophilia.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of eosinophilia such as strongyloidiasis and toxocariasis
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood films (including concentration techniques) for microfilariae
Skin snip examination for M. streptocerca microfilariae
Full blood count to detect eosinophilia
Species identification of microfilariae by morphology or molecular methods
Screening for co-infection with other filariae, particularly Loa loa before treatment
Serological or antigen tests where available to support diagnosis
redFlags: Marked eosinophilia with systemic symptoms warranting exclusion of other pathology
Co-infection with Loa loa raising the risk of treatment-related reactions
Serositis or effusions attributable to the parasite
Persistent symptoms despite therapy suggesting alternative or additional diagnoses
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally very good, as most infections are benign and asymptomatic; symptomatic disease usually responds to appropriate species-directed therapy, though clearance of adult worms can be slow.
pitfalls: Attributing all symptoms to Mansonella when co-infection with other filariae is common
Treating without first excluding heavy Loa loa co-infection
Missing the diagnosis because microfilariae require the correct sampling method and timing
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Direct antiparasitic therapy by species, using diethylcarbamazine for M. streptocerca and M. ozzardi where appropriate
Use doxycycline to target Wolbachia endosymbionts for M. perstans, which responds poorly to diethylcarbamazine
Consider ivermectin for its activity against M. ozzardi microfilariae
Screen for and exclude Loa loa co-infection before microfilaricidal treatment to avoid severe reactions
Provide symptomatic relief with antihistamines and analgesia for pruritus, transient swellings and arthralgia
Reassure and observe asymptomatic individuals in whom microfilariae are an incidental finding
Refer to infectious diseases or tropical medicine for species confirmation and treatment planning
